entities.name: Invasive aPWV
observations: Lower baseline invasive aortic pulse wave velocity was associated with greater blood-pressure response after renal sympathetic denervation in small clinical cohorts.
A 14.4 m/s threshold showed larger 3-month ambulatory systolic BP reductions below the threshold, but the cutoff lacks robust independent validation.
Evidence addresses short-term BP response, not hard cardiovascular or renal outcomes.

entities.name: Renal sympathetic denervation
observations: Invasive aPWV has been studied as a predictor of blood-pressure response after renal sympathetic denervation, primarily in treatment-resistant hypertension cohorts.

entities.name: PMID:27497368
observations: In a 58-patient final analysis, responders had lower invasive aPWV than nonresponders (14.4±4.4 vs 17.7±4.5 m/s; p=0.009); invasive PWV was the only significant multivariable predictor of response.
The study used 6-month ambulatory BP response and concluded that lower PWV might help select RDN candidates.

entities.name: PMID:35244604
observations: In 80 patients, invasive PWV below 14.4 m/s was associated with larger 3-month 24-hour and daytime systolic BP reductions than high iPWV.
The abstract leaves ambiguity about whether iPWV itself was independently validated versus ascending-aortic distensibility and baseline systolic BP.

entities.name: PMID:29744617
observations: In 32 analyzable patients, below-median invasive PWV was associated with better RDN BP response; ROC AUC was 0.849 (p=0.004).
Small sample size and median-based classification limit precision and clinical generalizability.
